context_line: You will hear part of a lecture about how seed banks store and check plant seeds.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at seed banks — what they are for, how a seed actually gets into one, and why a surprising number of plants cannot go into one at all. Most of what I describe applies to crop plants and their wild relatives, because that is where the funding has been.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: The idea is older than people assume. The first collections kept deliberately for future breeding date from the nineteen twenties, and they were built by plant breeders who had noticed that the varieties they wanted to work with were disappearing from farms. What changed in the nineteen seventies was the cold store. Before that, a collection had to be grown out every few years simply to stay alive.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: So: collection. A field team does not take every seed it can find, for two reasons. The first is obvious — you leave the population able to reproduce, and the convention is to take no more than a fifth of the seed that is ripe on the day you visit. The second reason is genetic. Collect from three plants and you capture almost none of the variation, so the guidance is to sample from at least fifty plants, spread across the whole stand, and to keep the seed from each plant separate until it reaches the store.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: You will hear thirty plants quoted, and that figure does appear in the older manuals, but the modelling done since points to fifty as the working minimum.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Everything that happens next is about removing water. A seed dried properly and kept cold respires so slowly that it barely respires at all. Drying is done in a room held at about fifteen degrees and fifteen per cent relative humidity, and it is deliberately slow, because seed dried too quickly on the outside forms a hard skin that traps water inside. Depending on the species, the seed leaves that room at around five per cent moisture.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Then it is sealed, and the seal matters more than the container. A jar with a poor gasket lets the seed take water back out of the air, and that seed is worse off than one never dried at all. Once sealed, the standard storage temperature is minus twenty degrees. You will still see minus eighteen quoted — the old domestic-freezer figure — but the international standard moved to minus twenty years ago.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Before anything is put away it is counted and checked. X-ray is now routine: it shows you at a glance which seeds are empty husks and which have an embryo inside. Then a sample is germinated, typically two hundred seeds, to establish a baseline. The threshold I was taught was seventy-five per cent, but it has been raised since: if fewer than eighty-five per cent come up, the collection is not accepted and it goes back to the field team.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: That baseline has to be repeated. Every accession is retested at intervals, and the interval most banks now work to is ten years. It was five, and for some species it still is, but testing consumes seed — every test takes two hundred seeds out of a store that may hold only a few thousand. When a retest falls below the threshold, the remaining seed is sown out and a fresh, larger batch is harvested. That process is called regeneration, and it is the most expensive thing a seed bank does.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Regeneration also carries a risk, which is why banks put it off as long as they safely can. Every time you grow a sample out you select: a few seeds do not germinate, a few cross with the neighbouring row. Do that often enough and the material in the jar is no longer the population that was collected. A seed bank is less a photograph than a photograph that fades a little every time you copy it.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Now, duplication. No serious collection keeps its only copy of anything in one building. The rule is that a duplicate goes to a second site, in a different country wherever that can be arranged, and that it is a separately packaged portion set aside at the outset, not a subsample of the same jar. The reason is mundane: the commonest cause of loss over the past fifty years has been a freezer failing quietly over a long weekend.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: Which brings me to the limitation. Everything I have described works for what are called orthodox seeds — seeds that tolerate drying and freezing. Many species have seeds that do not. Take the moisture content of an acorn down to five per cent and you have killed it. Those seeds are called recalcitrant, and they include oak, chestnut, mango, cocoa, rubber and most of the large-seeded trees of wet tropical forest. The figure usually given is that about eight per cent of the world's plant species are recalcitrant.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: For those species every option is more expensive. You can keep a living collection — an orchard, in effect — which takes land and is exposed to weather and to pests. You can freeze the embryo alone in liquid nitrogen, at minus a hundred and ninety-six degrees, which works for a growing number of species but has to be worked out one species at a time. Or you can hold tissue in slow growth in culture, which buys you a year or two rather than a century.

turns.speaker: F1
turns.text: For next week, read the two chapters and come with an answer to this. If you had a fixed budget and four hundred accessions overdue for regeneration, how would you decide which forty to do first? There is no correct answer, and I want to hear you defend an ordering.
